name: Paulo Roberto Falcão
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Brazilian Série A national championship with Internacional in 1975 at age 22, followed by repeat titles in 1976 and 1979, all by age 26.
early_history_summary: Falcão joined Internacional's youth academy in Porto Alegre at age 12 in 1965 and progressed through the ranks, turning professional in 1972 at age 19. He became a key midfielder for Internacional, leading the club to three Brazilian national championships (1975, 1976, 1979) and establishing himself as one of Brazil's elite players before his transfer to Roma in 1980.
family_context_summary: Falcão came from a working-class background in Abelardo Luz, Santa Catarina; he reportedly helped carry bricks at the construction site of Internacional's Beira-Rio stadium alongside his father.
primary_early_advantage_tags: youth academy, Brazilian football, early professional debut, working-class background
evidence_summary: Falcão joined Internacional's youth system at age 12 and turned professional at 19, winning three Brazilian national championships by 26. His early path was shaped by immersion in Brazil's elite club football pipeline rather than family resources. He came from a modest background in a small town and earned his place through demonstrated talent in the youth ranks. The Brazilian football ecosystem of the 1970s provided a high-level competitive platform that accelerated his development.

name: Bernard Arnault
milestone_by_age_26: Convinced his father to sell the construction division of Ferret-Savinel and pivot the family company to real estate in 1974 at age 25, generating 40 million French francs and renaming the company Férinel.
early_history_summary: Arnault graduated from the prestigious École Polytechnique in 1971 at age 22 and joined his father's civil engineering company Ferret-Savinel. Within three years, he persuaded his father to liquidate the construction arm and invest the proceeds into real estate, a strategic pivot that laid the financial foundation for his later luxury goods empire. He was effectively running the company by age 25.
family_context_summary: Arnault was born into a wealthy Catholic family in Roubaix; his father was an École Centrale graduate who owned the civil engineering company Ferret-Savinel, and his maternal grandfather Étienne Savinel had founded the company. His mother was a pianist with a fascination for Dior.
parent_family_domain_summary: Arnault's father owned and operated Ferret-Savinel, a civil engineering and construction company, providing direct business exposure and a ready-made platform for Bernard's early career. His grandfather founded the company, establishing a multi-generational family business.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family business, École Polytechnique, inherited company platform, father mentorship
evidence_summary: Arnault's early career was built on a powerful family-business platform: his father's company Ferret-Savinel, founded by his grandfather. After graduating from École Polytechnique, he joined the family firm and by age 25 had orchestrated a strategic pivot from construction to real estate, generating 40 million francs in capital. His father handed him operational control, citing confidence in his abilities. This inherited business infrastructure and capital base provided the foundation for his later acquisition of Boussac Saint-Frères and Christian Dior in 1984.

name: Mstislav Rostropovich
milestone_by_age_26: Won the gold medal at the Soviet Union's inaugural national competition for young musicians in 1945 at age 18, followed by first prizes at the Prague and Budapest International Music Awards (1947, 1949, 1950) and the Stalin Prize in 1950 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Rostropovich began studying piano with his mother at age four and cello with his father, a former pupil of Pablo Casals, at age eight. He entered the Moscow Conservatory at age 16 in 1943, where he studied composition with Shostakovich and Prokofiev. His competitive breakthrough came at 18 with the national gold medal, and by 23 he had received the Stalin Prize, the Soviet Union's highest distinction, while already teaching at the Leningrad and Moscow Conservatories.
family_context_summary: Rostropovich was born into a deeply musical family: his father Leopold was a renowned cellist and former student of Pablo Casals, and his mother Sofiya was an accomplished pianist. The family relocated during wartime but maintained intensive musical training.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were professional musicians who provided Rostropovich's foundational training: his father taught him cello from age eight and his mother taught him piano from age four. His father's direct lineage to Pablo Casals placed him in an elite pedagogical tradition from the start.
primary_early_advantage_tags: musical family, Casals lineage, Moscow Conservatory, Shostakovich mentorship, early competition wins
evidence_summary: Rostropovich's extraordinary early career was built on deep family-domain apprenticeship: both parents were professional musicians, with his father trained by Pablo Casals. He began cello at age eight, entered the Moscow Conservatory at 16, and won the national gold medal at 18. By 23, he held the Stalin Prize and was teaching at two conservatories. His access to elite mentors (Shostakovich, Prokofiev) and the Soviet musical infrastructure provided rare developmental depth. Wartime displacement created adversity but also urgency in his training.

name: José Feliciano
milestone_by_age_26: Signed to RCA Records at age 18 in 1963, released debut album 'The Voice & Guitar of José Feliciano' at 19 in 1964, and scored a #3 Billboard Hot 100 hit with 'Light My Fire' in 1968 at age 23, winning Grammy Awards for Best New Artist and Best Contemporary Male Pop Vocal Performance.
early_history_summary: Born blind in rural Puerto Rico, Feliciano taught himself guitar by listening to records, practicing up to 14 hours a day. His family moved to New York City when he was five. By age 16, he was performing on the Greenwich Village coffeehouse circuit, and at 17 he quit school to perform full-time. He was discovered at Gerde's Folk City and signed to RCA in 1963, releasing his first album the following year and breaking through internationally with 'Light My Fire' in 1968.
family_context_summary: Feliciano was born into a poor Puerto Rican family as one of eleven children; his father was a farmer who later worked as a longshoreman in New York. The family lived in Spanish Harlem after immigrating when José was five. He was born blind due to congenital glaucoma.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of musical family background. Feliciano was largely self-taught, learning from records.
primary_early_advantage_tags: blindness, self-taught, Greenwich Village, poverty, immigrant, 14-hour practice
evidence_summary: Feliciano's path was defined by extreme adversity and self-creation: born blind in poverty, he taught himself guitar from records with obsessive 14-hour daily practice sessions. His family's immigration to New York placed him near the Greenwich Village folk scene, where he began performing professionally at 16. His blindness and poverty created urgency and a distinctive musical voice blending flamenco, folk, and Latin styles. He was discovered at Gerde's Folk City and signed to RCA at 18, with his breakthrough hit 'Light My Fire' arriving at 23. No family resources or connections facilitated his rise.

name: Jeff Bezos
milestone_by_age_26: Became the youngest senior vice president at D.E. Shaw & Co., a prominent Wall Street investment firm, in 1990 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Bezos graduated from Princeton University in 1986 at age 22 with a BSE in electrical engineering and computer science, summa cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa. He worked at Fitel (a fintech startup), then Bankers Trust, before joining the hedge fund D.E. Shaw & Co., where he rose to become the firm's youngest senior vice president at age 26 in 1990. This Wall Street experience and financial acumen laid the groundwork for his founding of Amazon in 1994.
family_context_summary: Bezos was born to a teenage mother in Albuquerque and was adopted by his Cuban-American stepfather Miguel Bezos, an Exxon engineer. The family moved to Houston and then Miami, providing a middle-class upbringing. His grandfather's Texas ranch fostered self-reliance and mechanical curiosity.
parent_family_domain_summary: No direct family-domain advantage in technology or business; his stepfather was an engineer at Exxon, providing a middle-class stable environment. His grandfather influenced his practical tinkering instincts but was not a domain expert.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Princeton, EE/CS degree, Wall Street, D.E. Shaw, early computer access
evidence_summary: Bezos's early trajectory was driven by elite institutional credentials: Princeton summa cum laude in electrical engineering and computer science, followed by rapid advancement on Wall Street. His middle-class family provided stability but not extraordinary resources. His early interest in computers and space (president of Princeton's SEDS chapter) combined with quantitative skills to make him valuable at D.E. Shaw, where he became youngest SVP at 26. The late-1980s Wall Street tech boom provided the structural wave that accelerated his career.

name: Jürgen Klinsmann
milestone_by_age_26: Became a regular starter in the Bundesliga (top German division) at VfB Stuttgart from 1984 at age 20, scoring 15 goals in his first Bundesliga season, and was a prolific scorer through age 26, culminating in winning the 1990 FIFA World Cup with West Germany.
early_history_summary: Klinsmann began playing organized football at age 8 with TB Gingen, scoring 106 goals in 18 games as a child. He moved through SC Geislingen and then Stuttgarter Kickers' youth program, signing a professional contract at 16 in 1981. He played in the 2. Bundesliga for Stuttgarter Kickers (1981-1984), scoring 19 goals in the 1983-84 season, then transferred to VfB Stuttgart in the top-flight Bundesliga in 1984, where he scored 15 goals in his first season and became one of the league's top strikers.
family_context_summary: Klinsmann was one of four sons of a master baker, Siegfried Klinsmann, who bought a bakery in Stuttgart when Jürgen was 14. The family was middle-class; his parents wanted him to complete a bakery apprenticeship as a fallback, which he did in 1982.
parent_family_domain_summary: No football-domain advantage in the family; his father was a baker. However, the family's move to Stuttgart when Klinsmann was 14 placed him near the city's professional clubs, which facilitated his signing with Stuttgarter Kickers.
primary_early_advantage_tags: German football system, youth clubs, early professional debut, Bundesliga, prolific scorer
evidence_summary: Klinsmann's early career was built on Germany's structured football pipeline: he joined organized football at 8, was spotted in regional selections, and signed a professional contract at 16 with Stuttgarter Kickers. His family's move to Stuttgart when he was 14 was pivotal, placing him near professional clubs. He completed a bakery apprenticeship as a fallback but quickly established himself as a prolific scorer, reaching the Bundesliga at 20 and becoming a World Cup winner at 26. His childhood goal-scoring record (106 goals in 18 games) suggests early natural striking ability.

name: Hans Georg Dehmelt
milestone_by_age_26: Completed his diplom (master's equivalent) at Göttingen in 1948 at age 26, but his PhD came in 1950 at age 28 and his significant scientific contributions (NQR co-discovery, ion trap experiments) came after age 26; no material independently verifiable milestone found by 26.
early_history_summary: Dehmelt grew up in Berlin during the Depression, developing an interest in radios and physics. He attended the Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster on scholarship, then served in the army during WWII. He was ordered to study physics at the University of Breslau in 1943, then resumed graduate studies at Göttingen after the war, completing his diplom in 1948 and PhD in 1950.
evidence_summary: Dehmelt's early career was disrupted by WWII; he completed his diplom at Göttingen at age 26 in 1948, which represents standard academic progression rather than a material milestone. His PhD followed in 1950 at age 28, and his co-discovery of nuclear quadrupole resonance and subsequent ion trap work came after age 26. No independently verifiable material milestone was identified by age 26.

name: Svetlana Alexievich
milestone_by_age_26: Was working as a local newspaper journalist in Belarus by age 26, but her first book 'War's Unwomanly Face' was not finished until 1983 at age 35 and published in 1985; no material independently verifiable milestone found by 26.
early_history_summary: Alexievich grew up in Belarus as the daughter of schoolteachers. After finishing school, she worked as a reporter for a local newspaper, then studied journalism at Minsk University from 1967 to 1972, graduating at age 24. She then worked at local newspapers in Beresa and later Minsk, developing her interview-based documentary style over many years before publishing her first book in 1985.
family_context_summary: Alexievich was born to a Belarusian father and Ukrainian mother, both schoolteachers, in a family with a grandfather who was also a rural schoolteacher. The family settled in a Belarusian village after her father's military service.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; her parents were schoolteachers, not writers or journalists, though the family valued education.
evidence_summary: Alexievich's early career consisted of standard journalism work at local Belarusian newspapers through her mid-twenties. She studied journalism at Minsk University (1967-1972) and then worked as a reporter. Her distinctive literary method developed slowly over many years, and her first book was not published until she was 37. No material milestone was identified by age 26; her fame arrived much later with the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2015.

name: Aldo Rossi
milestone_by_age_26: Was working as an editor at Casabella magazine and as an assistant at architectural studios in Milan by age 26, but his degree came at 27-28, his influential book 'The Architecture of the City' was published in 1966 at age 35, and his first major built work came in the late 1960s; no material independently verifiable milestone found by 26.
early_history_summary: Rossi enrolled at the Polytechnic University of Milan in 1949, began collaborating with the architectural magazine Casabella in 1955, and started working at the studio of Ignazio Gardella in 1956. He graduated in architecture in 1958-1959 at age 27-28, began teaching in 1963, and published his seminal work 'The Architecture of the City' in 1966. His first significant built projects came in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
family_context_summary: Rossi was born in Milan; his father was engaged in bicycle manufacturing, a business founded by his grandfather. He grew up during WWII and was educated at Catholic schools before entering architecture school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; the family business was bicycle manufacturing, not architecture or design.
evidence_summary: Rossi's early career involved editorial work at Casabella magazine and apprenticeship at established Milan studios, but these were positions rather than independent achievements. He did not complete his architecture degree until age 27-28, and his influential theoretical work and built projects all came after age 26. No material independently verifiable milestone was identified by age 26.

name: Elizabeth Blackburn
milestone_by_age_26: Was a PhD student at Cambridge's MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology working with Frederick Sanger by age 26, but her PhD was completed in 1975 at age 27 and her landmark telomere discoveries came as a postdoc at Yale in 1978 at age 30; no material independently verifiable milestone found by 26.
early_history_summary: Blackburn grew up in Tasmania, the daughter of two physicians. She earned a BSc in 1970 and MSc in 1972 from the University of Melbourne, then moved to Cambridge at age 24 for doctoral work with Frederick Sanger at the LMB. She was still a graduate student at age 26, completing her PhD on bacteriophage DNA sequencing in 1975 before moving to Yale as a postdoc.
family_context_summary: Blackburn was born in Hobart, Tasmania, to two family physicians, with a grandfather and great-grandfather who were geologists. The family valued science and intellectual pursuits. She was inspired by reading Marie Curie's biography as a child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were physicians, and earlier family members were geologists, creating a scientifically oriented family environment that encouraged her interest in science from a young age.
evidence_summary: Blackburn's early path was a standard academic progression: BSc and MSc at Melbourne, then PhD at Cambridge's LMB with Sanger. While the LMB was an elite environment, being a PhD student is not a material milestone. Her PhD was completed at 27, and her Nobel-winning telomere work came at 30 as a postdoc at Yale. No material independently verifiable milestone was identified by age 26.

name: Lotfi A. Zadeh
milestone_by_age_26: Had completed an MS from MIT in 1946 at age 25 and was an instructor at Columbia University working toward his PhD by age 26, but his PhD came in 1949 at age 28 and his seminal contributions (z-transform in 1952, fuzzy sets in 1965) came well after 26; no material independently verifiable milestone found by 26.
early_history_summary: Zadeh was born in Baku, Azerbaijan, and grew up in Iran. He earned a BS in electrical engineering from the University of Tehran in 1942, then moved to the US in 1944. He received an MS from MIT in 1946 and became an instructor at Columbia University while pursuing his PhD, which he completed in 1949 at age 28. His influential research on the z-transform and fuzzy sets came in the 1950s and 1960s.
family_context_summary: Zadeh was born in Baku, Azerbaijan, the son of a correspondent for Iranian newspapers. The family moved to Iran, where he attended Alborz College, an American Presbyterian missionary school in Tehran. He sold goods to the American Army during WWII to fund his move to the US.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of family background in engineering or science.
evidence_summary: Zadeh's early career followed a standard academic path: BS from Tehran, MS from MIT at 25, then instructor position at Columbia while pursuing PhD. His MS and instructorship represent normal academic progression rather than material milestones. His PhD was completed at 28, and his seminal research contributions (z-transform, fuzzy sets) came years later. No material independently verifiable milestone was identified by age 26.

name: Carlo Rubbia
milestone_by_age_26: Co-authored a paper published in Physical Review Letters in 1959 with W. Baker at Columbia University, measuring neutron asymmetry from muon capture in magnesium and demonstrating parity violation in weak interactions, at age 25.
early_history_summary: Rubbia grew up in wartime Italy, initially failing the entrance exam for the Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa but gaining admission when another student dropped out. He completed his degree with a thesis on cosmic ray experiments under Marcello Conversi, developing pulsed gas particle detectors. In 1958, he went to Columbia University as a postdoctoral researcher, where he co-authored a 1959 PRL paper on parity violation in muon capture. He then joined CERN around 1960, where he spent the remainder of his career.
family_context_summary: Rubbia was born in Gorizia, Italy; his family moved to Venice and then Udine due to wartime disruption. His father was an electrical engineer who encouraged him to study engineering, though Rubbia chose physics instead. As a child, he collected and experimented with abandoned military communications equipment.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was an electrical engineer, which may have influenced his technical interests, though the father preferred he study engineering rather than physics. The family was displaced by wartime events.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Scuola Normale, Columbia University, CERN, parity violation experiment, wartime displacement
evidence_summary: Rubbia's early career benefited from elite institutional access: the Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa for his degree, then Columbia University for postdoctoral work where he co-authored a PRL paper on parity violation at 25. His father's engineering background may have influenced his technical orientation. Wartime displacement and initially failing the Scuola Normale entrance exam created adversity but also serendipity when another student's withdrawal opened his place. The post-war particle physics boom provided the structural wave for his career.
